statement: ABCDE is a regular pentagon. A square ABFG is drawn on side AB, outside the pentagon, so that G is next to A. What is the size of angle AEG?

choices.misconception: I found angle EAG is 162° and that the other two angles of triangle AEG share 18°, but forgot to split the 18° between them.
I used the pentagon's 108° angle at A as the top of triangle AEG and ignored the square's angle.
I found angle EAG is 162° and halved it, mixing up the top angle with the base angles.
I found angle EAG at the corner A and gave that, instead of the angle at E.

hints: Draw it, and look at the angles meeting at A.
The angles around point A add up to 360°. Once you know the angle at A in triangle AEG, look at which sides of that triangle are equal.
Around A: 108° from the pentagon, 90° from the square, and the rest is angle EAG. Also AE = AB = AG.

solutions.reliable: Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°, and the square's angle at A is 90°. The angles around A add to 360°, so angle EAG is 360° - 108° - 90° = 162°. The pentagon and the square share side AB, so AE = AB = AG and triangle AEG is isosceles. Its two base angles share 180° - 162° = 18°, so each is 9°. The transferable idea: when two regular shapes share a side, equal sides appear, and isosceles triangles turn one angle into all three.

whyOnTest: Angle chasing with two regular shapes tests two facts in a row: angles around a point and the equal sides they share.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
